passage: “Hemant, honestly, I nearly did it. I'm Sachin. I got a message saying my card had a problem and I should confirm my details through a link. The page looked real, and I had half of my card number typed before something stopped me. It was the little voice that said, why would a bank text me a link? I closed it. Then I didn't just delete it. I took a screenshot and showed my parents at dinner. Nobody shouted. Dad found the official cybercrime website and we reported it together, and Mum phoned the bank on the number on the back of the card, so they could watch for anything odd. It felt better than pretending nothing had happened.”

qa.q: What did Sachin take a screenshot of?
qa.a: The message asking for card details.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel at the moment before closing the page?
qa.a: Tempted and rushed, then uneasy enough to stop when the little voice asked why a bank would send a link.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do, and why?
qa.a: Warn friends about the message, since scammers often send the same one to many people.

qa.q: How does this look to Sachin's parents?
qa.a: They are relieved that Sachin told them instead of quietly deleting the message, and glad to report it and tell the bank so it can watch for odd activity.

grounding: After a suspicious link asking for card details, a teen tells parents, screenshots the message and they report it to the cybercrime portal and bank.

subtype: Approach: reporting to parents and the official cybercrime channel [Action]
passage:
I'm Abhinav, Hemant's cousin, and I was staying with them that weekend. On Saturday night Hemant came into the living room holding his phone out as if it were hot. A message said his mother's card would stop working unless he “updated details” at a link. He'd opened the link and seen a page asking for the card number, but typed nothing.
He didn't delete it. He took screenshots of the message and the page first, then showed his parents. His father wrote down the sender's number as Hemant read it out. His mother called the bank on the number from her card and told them about the message. Then the three of them sat at the computer and filled in a complaint on the national cybercrime reporting website, attaching the screenshots.
It took about forty minutes. Hemant looked tired but steady by the end.

qa.q: What did Hemant do before showing his parents?
qa.a: He took screenshots of the message and the page.

qa.q: How might Hemant have been feeling when he walked in holding the phone out?
qa.a: He was likely alarmed and uneasy, holding the phone as if it were hot, after seeing a page ask for card details.

qa.q: Why was reporting better than quietly deleting the message?
qa.a: Reporting with screenshots warns the bank and helps the authorities trace the sender, which can protect other families too.

qa.q: How might Hemant's mother see what her son did?
qa.a: She would likely be relieved nothing was typed and grateful he told them at once, so she could alert the bank that night.

grounding: A cousin sees a teen screenshot a phishing message, tell his parents, and report it with them to the bank and the national cybercrime website.

passage:
Monday: A text reaches Chinmay: “Your parcel is on hold. Pay the redelivery charge here.” The link opens a page asking for card details. He closes it and nearly deletes the message, feeling foolish for tapping at all.
Tuesday: At breakfast he mentions it to his sister Gopika, who works at a bank branch. “Don't delete it,” she says. “Screenshot it. Tell Amma and Appa tonight.” That evening he shows all three the screenshots. Appa rings the helpline on the back of his card to check nothing has been used. Then Chinmay and Gopika fill in a report on the national cybercrime portal, attaching the screenshots and the sender's number.
Friday: A reference number arrives by email, and the bank confirms the family's cards are safe. Chinmay pins the reference number on the fridge.

qa.q: What did the link ask for?
qa.a: The page asked for card details.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay nearly delete the message on Monday?
qa.a: He felt foolish and a bit ashamed for tapping the link at all, and deleting it seemed a way to make the mistake disappear.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay do if he had already typed the card number?
qa.a: Tell Amma and Appa at once so the bank can block the card straight away; speed matters more than embarrassment.

qa.q: How does the week look to Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika probably feels proud that one breakfast conversation turned into a proper report and a safe outcome for the family.

grounding: Shows a teen telling his family about a phishing link, keeping screenshots, and reporting it with them to the bank and the national cybercrime portal.
